correctness.rationale: For 1/2<p<1, the analytic proof computes derivatives of the two branches of H(x)=KL(Bernoulli(p)||Bernoulli(x)), proves (1-p)/p<v/u<1 and strict decay of v/u with energy via an explicit positive quadratic J_r. The logit-to-energy Jacobian is exactly 1/u and 1/v, so the beta mean tail is a strict monotone expectation under exponential tilting. Symmetry handles p<=1/2, and concentration endpoints follow from integrability on finite energy intervals and divergence of the full logit measure. The binomial–beta identity has the exact parameters (nt-1,1/n,t-1) and shapes ((n-1)t,t). The standalone checker in this package returned 600 rational tail checks, 576 exact consecutive inequalities and 3469 exact derivative tests. All real-parameter quantifiers rest on the analytic argument, not the finite tests.

originality.rationale: The paper of Babichenko et al. gives the exact binomial-infimum claim as an unproved conjecture (arXiv:2312.01874v1, Remark 2). The new proportional-beta sign result proves all its integer instances. Hornik's (2024) fixed-other-shape monotonicity, Karp's individual-parameter log-concavity, and Leobacher–Steinicke's (2026) one-shape monotonicity do not control joint proportional growth. Targeted source/equivalence searches, original-paper text comparisons, and accessible scientific database summaries revealed no covering theorem. Earlier uncatalogued equivalent statements remain a residual historical priority risk.
residual_risks: Historical priority risk: an older or differently indexed proportional-beta concentration theorem could subsume the claim despite the direct primary-source comparisons.
Database search coverage and a model's literature inspection do not constitute an independent proof of originality.

value.rationale: The exact finite-n expression is an explicitly motivated unproved conjecture in Babichenko et al., Remark 2, with a stated exact threshold consequence for matroid-rank quantile feasibility. Proving strict monotonicity for all n>=3 settles the natural entire sequence and yields a universal continuous-concentration beta distribution theorem, with correct boundary n=2. The result is not a mere restatement of existing fixed-shape beta inequalities, and the exact quantitative threshold has a specific mathematical use beyond a tiny numerical improvement.
